title: How Whale Sharks Work
summary: Josh and Chuck open with a Discovery Shark Week promotional package (a jar of bloody shorts, shark tooth keychain, and a mock obituary for Chief Brody) and the Frenzied Waters site. They then discuss whale sharks: their size, gentle filter-feeding on plankton and krill, the Georgia Aquarium exhibit and its Taiwan sourcing, the fishing and shark finning trade, the economic value of ecotourism, and the slow reproductive age and pup counts. Discussion covers swimming with whale sharks, "soft encounters," humpback whales, dolphins, and the debate over ecotourism. Closing segments cover a Varanasi-area holy man's blessing that reportedly halted whale shark fishing in India, Shark Week plugs, and a listener mail about being born with toxoplasmosis.

segments.title: Opening banter and Shark Week promo package
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck banter, then describe a Discovery Shark Week promotional package: a jar with bloody shorts, shark tooth keychain, and a mock obituary for Chief Brody. They point listeners to Frenzied Waters and Shark Week.

segments.title: Swimming with whale sharks at the Georgia Aquarium
segments.summary: The hosts recount swimming with whale sharks, a manta ray, hammerhead sharks and a grouper at the Georgia Aquarium, describing the whale sharks' graceful movement and their avoidance of touching the hosts.

segments.title: Whale shark size, range and migration
segments.summary: Chuck explains that whale sharks are the largest fish in the sea, can reach over sixty feet, live in warm waters except the Mediterranean, and occasionally appear in unexpected places such as off Mississippi and Louisiana, where a fisherman's boat became a research vessel.

segments.title: Captivity, Taiwan fishing and ecotourism economics
segments.summary: The hosts discuss the Georgia Aquarium exhibit, which reportedly sourced whale sharks from Taiwan, and how the aquarium's relationship with Taiwan reportedly reduced its kill quota. They compare the low payout for killing a whale shark with the estimated value of ecotourism.

segments.title: Shark finning, reproduction and population
segments.summary: The hosts describe shark finning, the slow reproductive age of whale sharks (around twenty-five to thirty years), litters of up to 300 pups, and population estimates of roughly 500,000 with vulnerable conservation status.

segments.title: Whale shark feeding and soft encounters
segments.summary: Chuck explains that whale sharks are filter feeders eating plankton, krill and small shrimp, and that they cough up food too large to pass. The hosts discuss soft encounters, humpback whales in Tonga and the Dominican Republic, and dolphin swimming.

segments.title: Ecotourism debate and Indian holy man
segments.summary: The hosts debate the ethics of ecotourism versus killing sharks and note concerns that chumming disrupts reef sharks. They then recount how a holy man, Murari Bapu, blessed a netted whale shark in India, which reportedly halted local whale shark fishing.

segments.title: Scuba diving and closing plugs
segments.summary: Josh describes scuba diving with the sharks and the exhaustion it caused, then the hosts point listeners to Frenzied Waters, Shark Week, and the Blood in the Water special.

segments.title: Listener mail on toxoplasmosis
segments.summary: A listener writes that he was born to a mother with toxoplasmosis and was told he might not develop a head, and reflects on how toxoplasmosis behaviors match his family. Josh and Chuck respond and give the address for listener mail.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: The episode ends with a closing promotion for How Stuff Works forward thinking content and sponsor read.
